articles.title: International Olympic Committee scraps gender equality, diversity and inclusion panel in major reshuffle
articles.summary: The International Olympic Committee is eliminating its Gender Equality, Diversity and Inclusion Commission months after adopting new sex eligibility rules.
articles.body: The International Olympic Committee (IOC) is eliminating its Gender Equality, Diversity and Inclusion Commission, as the organization undergoes cultural changes under its new president Kirsty Coventry. Under Coventry, the most notable change came earlier this year, when the IOC explicitly banned biological males from women's sports. This week's cuts come as part of a restructuring that will replace 12 permanent advisory bodies with smaller working groups assembled to address specific issues. Friday’s announcement comes months after the IOC adopted new eligibility rules reserving women’s Olympic events for biological females beginning with the 2028 Los Angeles Games, a policy addressing a central issue in the debate over fairness and safety in women’s sports. KAILLIE HUMPHRIES: IDENTITY IS NOT THE SAME AS BIOLOGY. THE SUPREME COURT AGREES The IOC’s Advisory Committee on Human Rights is also being discontinued, alongside commissions covering sustainability, technology, education and commercial partnerships. The organization said the changes followed more than a year of consultation and review. According to The Associated Press, the overhaul is a streamlining and cost-cutting measure that leaves 19 committees in place. The outgoing groups typically included between 10 and 30 members who gathered annually in Lausanne, Switzerland. The IOC said in an official announcement that the new arrangement would enable "more targeted engagement on key strategic priorities and policy development." Its Athletes’ Commission, Ethics Commission, Audit Committee and other institutional bodies will continue operating. Under President Kirsty Coventry, the IOC has already used a smaller expert group to examine eligibility for women’s competition. According to AP, the panel’s membership was kept confidential, and the review proceeded outside the gender equality and inclusion commission now being eliminated. The resulting policy, announced March 26, requires a one-time screening for the SRY gene, which is typically associated with male sex development. It excludes transgender women from female Olympic events and also affects some athletes with differences in sex development, with limited exceptions. The rules do not apply retroactively or to recreational sports. Coventry defended the policy as necessary to protect competition. "It would not be fair for biological males to compete in the female category," she said when the rules were announced. She also emphasized athletes’ dignity, access to counseling and medical guidance. SUPREME COURT MAKES RULING ON TRANS ATHLETES IN WOMEN'S SPORTS The policy aligns with President Donald Trump’s push for sex-based eligibility in women’s sports. His February 2025 executive order directed the secretary of state to press the IOC to adopt standards based on sex rather than gender identity or testosterone reduction. The IOC’s approach has drawn sharply different responses. Reem Alsalem, the United Nations special rapporteur on violence against women and girls, welcomed the eligibility policy as protecting female athletes’ fairness and safety. Human Rights Watch opposed mandatory genetic screening, arguing it threatens privacy and can expose women with variations in sex characteristics to discrimination. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Friday’s restructuring follows a pause in the affected commissions’ work that began in February. The IOC said it will now bring together experts through working groups with clearly defined assignments to guide future decisions.

articles.title: Ansel Haugsjaa, Chevonne Forgan win 2 titles at USA Luge's national start championships
articles.summary: (AP) — Ansel Haugsjaa and Chevonne Forgan went to the Olympics last winter as doubles sliders. They did just fine on their own in the season's opening race.
articles.body:
LAKE PLACID, N.Y. (AP) — Ansel Haugsjaa and Chevonne Forgan went to the Olympics last winter as doubles sliders. They did just fine on their own in the season's opening race.

Haugsjaa and Forgan pulled off rare feats by claiming titles in both singles and doubles races at USA Luge's national start championships, which are considered the unofficial start of the team's competitive season.

It was a night for doubles sliders to shine. Haugsjaa took the men's singles crown, then paired with Olympic teammate Marcus Mueller — who was second in the singles race, tied with fellow doubles specialist Zack DiGregorio — for their second national men's doubles start title in the last three years. Forgan claimed the women's singles title, before joining her Olympic teammate Sophia Kirkby to successfully defend their doubles start title.

"Showing up first and second in the singles race, we were feeling good going into doubles," Haugsjaa said. "I was shocked by how comfortable and easy it felt going back on the doubles sled after doing singles. Felt like I was right back at home, so it was really nice."

Mueller and Haugsjaa, who were world champions at the junior level, led the Olympic doubles race at Cortina d'Ampezzo, Italy in February, before a mistake in the second run sent them to a sixth-place finish.

Their success in singles on Friday doesn't have them thinking about trying those races more often.

"I think we're going to stick with doubles," Mueller said. "We made that decision a few years ago, to stick with doubles because we thought we can do a lot better. And with how close it was in these recent Olympics, I think we're really going to go for gold."

Same goes for Forgan, whose singles win seemed to catch her by surprise.

"Singles is scary," Forgan said. "Singles definitely poses interesting challenges."

A slew of past champions and Olympic veterans were not in Friday's race. Tucker West, a 13-time national start champion, retired after last season. Olympic women's singles racer Summer Britcher did not slide while recovering from injury, and longtime U.S. team member and Olympic veteran Emily Fischnaller has not revealed her future plans.

The World Cup season starts Nov. 28-29 in Winterberg, Germany.

articles.title: La dura batalla de una atleta olímpica contra la encefalomielitis miálgica: "He perdido mi independencia y mi salud"
articles.standfirst: Beth Dobbin, que se retiró del atletismo en abril, cuenta su día a día con esta enfermedad
articles.summary: Beth Dobbin, que se retiró del atletismo en abril, cuenta su día a día con esta enfermedad
articles.body: La atleta Beth Dobbin anunció en abril su retirada. A los 31 años, la semifinalista olímpica en los 200 de Tokio y bronce en el 4x400 con Escocia en los Juegos de la Commonwealth de 2022 ponía fin a su vida como deportista por una enfermedad de la que no dio más detalles. "Puede que no me retire del deporte con una medalla olímpica, pero me retiro con muchos sueños cumplidos", comentó entonces. Dobbin ha relatado ahora, en una entrevista con la BBC, todo el proceso que vivió hasta conocer que padece encefalomielitis miálgica, una enfermedad que provoca trastornos del sueño, déficit cognitivo, dolor y fatiga intensa. "He hecho cosas tan simples como ir al médico para un análisis de sangre y luego haber estado en cama durante meses. Es devastador, no puedo ni expresarlo con palabras. Todavía tengo a mi familia, pero he perdido mi independencia, mi salud, la capacidad de trabajar, la capacidad de hacer ejercicio", afirma Dobbin. La escocesa ha decidido contar su experiencia para dar visibilidad a esta dolencia y ayudar a quienes la padecen. Considera que su condición de deportista le otorga una plataforma para concienciar sobre una enfermedad que, según denuncia, todavía genera incomprensión. "Muchas personas que padecen esta enfermedad con las que he hablado me han dicho: 'No me creen, la gente piensa que soy un vago'. Nunca he conocido a nadie que no me crea, y eso se debe a que, ¿por qué un atleta dejaría de entrenar de repente después de 20 años?". La plusmarquista escocesa de los 200 metros empezó a encontrarse mal hace cinco años. A finales de 2021 y principios de 2022 tuvo varias veces Covid y una mononucleosis infecciosa. Empezó a dormir menos y apareció el dolor en las glándulas del cuello y las axilas. Los médicos de la Federación Británica de Atletismo le realizaron pruebas, pero no dieron un resultado relevante. Se achacó a una mononucleosis infecciosa persistente. Dobbin disputó el Mundial, los Juegos de la Commonwealth y el Europeo. En el Mundial sufrió de dolor de garganta y se despertaba a horas inusuales durante la noche. En los Juegos de la Commonwealth, se mareaba al correr y sentía más dolores musculares de lo normal. En el Campeonato Europeo, tuvo una salida en falso tras perder la sensibilidad en las piernas mientras estaba en los tacos de salida. Dobbin sufrió un grave deterioro de su salud tras los Europeos. Llegó a tener dificultades para ponerse en pie y pasaba gran parte del día en la cama. Tras varios intentos fallidos de volver a entrenar, consultó a diferentes especialistas hasta conocer el alcance de su enfermedad. El diagnóstico fue síndrome de fatiga crónica o encefalomielitis miálgica. Dobbin rechaza el término 'fatiga crónica' porque considera que minimiza la gravedad de la enfermedad. "Ojalá solo fuera fatiga, sería pan comido. Pero es mucho más que eso. Si incluyera la fatiga entre mis 20 síntomas principales, probablemente entraría en la lista". Dobbin relata también los problemas que sufrió para tratar la enfermedad. Tuvo que esperar 22 meses antes de conseguir una cita presencial con un especialista privado que ella misma buscó después de que finalizara su financiación por parte de la Federación Británica de Atletismo. La escocesa reconoce que su futuro es "muy sombrío" debido a una enfermedad que sigue sin tener cura. Sin embargo, confía en que la mayor atención médica y la financiación de la investigación tras la aparición de la COVID-19 y el covid persistente permitan avanzar en su tratamiento.

articles.title: Un club francés incluye un mapa del tesoro en su camiseta y dará 10.000 euros a quien encuentre el botín
articles.standfirst: El Royan Atlantique Volley-Ball, conocido como los 'Piratas', debuta en la máxima competición del voleibol francés
articles.summary: El Royan Atlantique Volley-Ball conocido como los 'Piratas', debuta en la máxima competición del voleibol francés
articles.body: El Royan Atlantique Volley-Ball ascendió esta temporada a Alterna Volstar, la máxima división del voleibol francés. El equipo, conocido como los Piratas, ha querido dar sentido a este sobrenombre con la búsqueda de un tesoro al que se llega gracias al mapa impreso en las camisetas de la primera equipación. De acuerdo con la Editorial Maison, una serie de acertijos se han incorporado a la indumentaria negra con ribetes amarillos. La resolución de estos enigmas conduce a un lugar de Francia donde se esconde una estatuilla. El primero que dé con ella será recompensado con 10.000 euros por parte del Royan Atlantique Volley-Ball (RAVB). Para hacerse valedor al premio deberá explicar también su método deductivo, acertijo por acertijo, para llegar hasta el tesoro. "La validación se basa en la precisión del razonamiento, nunca en el estilo. La más mínima irregularidad conlleva la descalificación", se lee en las reglas del juego. Los jugadores del Royan lucirán sus nuevas camisetas este sábado por la noche en el primer partido de su historia en la máxima categoría del voleibol francés contra el Montpellier, vigente campeón (21:00). Quien quiera acceder al juego puede comprar la equipación a través de la página web del equipo por 69 euros. "Uno de mis mejores amigos creó una empresa de búsquedas del tesoro para promocionar la región, y pensamos que sería divertido hacer una con nuestra camiseta. La primera temporada, terminamos últimos en la Ligue B; no era el momento adecuado. Hace unos meses, cuando vimos que íbamos a tener una temporada bastante buena, nos lanzamos", explica David Guelle, el presidente del Royan, en declaraciones a L'Equipe. El RAVB, que solía vender entre 200 y 300 camisetas al año en la Ligue B, encargó la fabricación de 600 esta temporada. Se entregarán en una caja con un pequeño folleto explicativo. El primer enigma es: ¿Cómo se lee la camiseta? "Es una búsqueda difícil, con varias etapas. Esperamos que mantenga a los participantes entretenidos durante unos meses", señala Guelle. Durante su primera temporada profesional en la Ligue B, el club ya puso en marcha otra búsqueda del tesoro para encontrar una calavera dorada enterrada en una playa de la ciudad. El premio, dos entradas VIP para un partido, fue entregado a los 10 días.

articles.title: Tola, campeón olímpico, gana el maratón de Pekín con récord de la prueba
articles.standfirst: El etíope corrió en 2.03:10, el tiempo más rápido de una prueba en suelo chino. En féminas, el triunfo fue para otra etíope, Anchinalu Dessie
articles.summary: El etíope corrió en 2.03:10, el tiempo más rápido de una prueba en suelo chino. En féminas, el triunfo fue para otra etíope, Anchinalu Dessie
articles.body: El etíope Tamirat Tola, oro olímpico en París 2024, se coronó este domingo campeón de la 44º edición del maratón de Pekín con un tiempo de 2.03:10, lo que supone un nuevo récord no solo para este evento sino para cualquiera de esta categoría celebrado sobre suelo chino. La mejor marca en Pekín la tenía desde 2019 el keniano Mathew Kisorio (2.07:06 segundos) y la de China databa de la carrera de 2023 en Shanghái, de la mano de otro keniano como Philimon Kiptoo Kipchumba (2.05:35). En la categoría femenina, el mejor tiempo de este domingo lo marcó también una etíope, Anchinalu Dessie: 2.20:36 segundos. Más de 32.000 participantes -140 de ellos, profesionales- tomaron las calles de la capital china en un recorrido que arrancó en la céntrica plaza de Tiananmen y finalizó en la zona olímpica de Pekín 2008. El mejor corredor local fue Li Dalin (2.08:30 segundos), situado actualmente en la posición número 440 del 'ranking' mundial de maratonianos. El maratón de Pekín se celebra de forma anual en la capital china desde 1981 y es considerada como la más prestigiosa del país asiático. Tras tres años de parón por la estricta política nacional de 'cero covid', la competición se reanudó en 2022, aunque ese año estuvo limitada únicamente a corredores locales, permitiendo la participación de atletas internacionales a partir de la siguiente edición.

articles.title: Track Cycling World Championships: Emma Finucane will 'come back fighting' after narrowly missing gold in Shanghai
articles.summary: Emma Finucane says she will "come back fighting" for gold medals after narrowly missing out on the top step in the Keirin.
articles.body:
Emma Finucane said she will "come back fighting" for gold medals after narrowly missing out on the top step of the podium for the third time at the Track Cycling World Championships , external in Shanghai.

Finucane, 23, was forced to settle for bronze in Sunday's keirin after being pipped to the finish line by neutral athlete Alina Lysenko and Lea Friedrich of Germany after leading into the home straight.

She finished just 14 thousandths of a second off top spot, with her bronze adding to silver medals won in the team sprint and individual sprint - both won by Chinese cyclists.

Finucane was part of Great Britain's team sprint gold medal-winning trio at the Paris Olympics in 2024 and Finucane says retaining that title in Los Angleles is the big aim.

She told BBC Sport: "To medal in all three races at the world champs, I'd never done that before.

"The confidence I have gained this week and the way I've been riding my bike, I can take that into the years to come.

"I'm actually really proud. I am frustrated not to be on the top step but I'll come back fighting. You can beat yourself up about races but I am learning all the time.

"Ultimately we are learning for the Olympics, that's a huge goal. I put myself in winning positions in every race and that's something I am proud of."

Finucane, who took bronze in both the individual sprint and keirin in Paris, won Britain's first Olympic gold in the women's team sprint alongside Katy Marchant and Sophie Capewell.

In Shanghai, Rhianna Parris-Smith replaced the newly-retired Marchant in the team which was beaten by Chinese trio Jiang Yulu, Tong Mengqi and Yuan Liying.

Finucane says the strength in depth inside the British team will drive them to success at the LA Games in 2028.

She said: "We won the team sprint in Paris which is one of the best moments of my life and there are 10 girls back at home fighting to be in the team. That's how we progress, and we will build on the momentum of this silver medal.

"Internal competition is how we win bike races. World records keep falling, we are pushing each other and it's really exciting."

Great Britain topped the medal table overall at the championships with 12 medals, including a hat-trick of gold medals for Anna Morris.

articles.title: Rhys McClenaghan: Olympic champion fails to make World Championship final
articles.summary: Olympic champion Rhys McClenaghan fails to reach the pommel horse final at the World Gymnastics Championships in Rotterdam.
articles.body:
Olympic champion Rhys McClenaghan failed to reach the pommel horse final at the World Gymnastics Championships in Rotterdam.

McClenaghan's score of 14.400 in qualifying was only good enough for a 10th place finish.

It has been a disappointing return to action for the 27-year-old, who missed the entirety of 2025 as he recovered from shoulder surgery.

A two-time world champion and three-time European gold medal winner, McClenaghan finished sixth in the Commonwealth Games in July which was his first major competition since his injury.

He was then forced to settle for seventh place at the Europeans in Zagreb in August.

articles.title: World Gymnastics Championships: Great Britain stars compete for Olympic places - how to watch, team details
articles.summary: Over 400 of the world's top artistic gymnasts from 84 nations compete at the World Championships in Rotterdam, this week, with Olympic spots up for grabs.
articles.body:
Over 400 of the world's top artistic gymnasts from 84 nations will compete at the 54th World Championships in Rotterdam from 20-25 October. Qualification places for the 2028 Olympics are up for grabs and you can watch the action live across the BBC.

The most prestigious competition in the calendar carries extra importance this year as the top three nations in each team event in the Netherlands will earn places at the Los Angeles 2028 Olympic Games.

China and Japan's men's teams start as favourites, while Great Britain retained the European title in August with a near-flawless display and could challenge for a medal.

The USA women have won every team final since 2011 and will be relying on the experience of Skye Blakely, who is competing at her fourth World Championships. This is a first senior Worlds for the rest of her team-mates, including Olympic team gold medallist Hezly Rivera.

The Russians, who are competing under neutral status, are European women's gold medallists, but reigning world all-around champion Angelina Melnikova was among three of their female gymnasts denied a visa to compete in Rotterdam.

Great Britain were fourth at the most recent Olympics and Europeans and are led by multiple major medallist Alice Kinsella, 13 months after she became a mother .

Reigning champion Daiki Hashimoto of Japan is vying for a fourth consecutive men's all-around world title, while Algerian Kaylia Nemour has a golden opportunity to become the first African winner in the women's event. Brilliant Brazilian Rebeca Andrade competes at a major global championships for the first time since her four-medal haul at the 2024 Olympics, which included gold on the floor.

Russian trio denied visas for world championships

The Olympic bronze medallist at Paris 2024 in floor is also a two-time world champion – in vault (2023) and floor (2025). The 24-year-old all-rounder did not compete in the European Championships this year or defend his titles at the Commonwealth Games in order to prepare for these World Championships.

Tulloch, 31, is affectionately known as Great Britain's 'King of the Rings'. He became the first British gymnast, and first black man, to win a World Championship medal on the apparatus in 2022.

Hepworth, 22, enjoyed a spectacular Olympic debut at Paris 2024, not only winning Team GB's first ever Olympic medal on the vault but also making history as the first Briton to make an Olympic rings final.

In 2019, Fraser won Great Britain's first-ever gold metal on the parallel bars at the World Championships. He then became Britain's first European all-around men's champion. Now 27, he remains a key figure in the team.

The 21-year-old made history this year as Scotland's first all-around Commonwealth Games champion, as well as claiming silver in the pommel horse. He makes his World Championships debut.

The Olympic bronze medallist returns after giving birth to her first child last year. She helped Team GB win their first Olympic women's team medal for 93 years at Tokyo 2020. This is the 25-year-old's sixth time competing at the World Championships.

The 34-year-old has competed in three Olympics and is a World, European and Commonwealth medallist. She has won three major golds and four silvers in the uneven bars.

At age 17, Evans became the first Welsh female artistic gymnast in 28 years to represent Team GB at the Olympic Games in Paris 2024. Now 19, she is already a Commonwealth gold medallist and a world silver medallist last year on floor.

Born and raised in Devon, the 18-year-old earned team, vault and floor silver medals at this year's Commonwealth Games. Martin was part of the fourth-placed British team at the Paris Olympics and she earned a world bronze medal in the floor event last year.

Leat, now 21, represented Great Britain at the 2025 European Championships and World Championships. She is the British champion in the balance beam and was part of the England team which won bronze at the 2026 Commonwealth Games.

articles.title: Asian Para Games: India win 11 medals on Day 1 as Nishad Kumar, Mona Agarwal lead four-gold haul
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: India made a spectacular start to the Asian Para Games, collecting 11 medals, including four gold, across shooting, athletics, judo and
articles.body: NEW DELHI: India made a spectacular start to the Asian Para Games, collecting 11 medals, including four gold, across shooting, athletics, judo and swimming on Monday to occupy fourth place in the overall standings.Established stars Mona Agarwal and Nishad Kumar led the charge, while middle-distance runner Soumya and javelin thrower Rinku also finished on top of the podium. India celebrated three 1-2 finishes, with compatriots sharing the gold and silver medals in shooting, athletics and javelin.The opening day also brought encouraging news from archery, table tennis and badminton, with Sheetal Devi matching the world record in the women’s compound qualification round and several Indian paddlers and shuttlers assuring themselves of medals by reaching the semifinals.Mona beats Avani in shooting thrillerThe medal rush began with a stirring comeback from Mona in the women’s 10m air rifle SH1 final. The Paris Paralympics bronze medallist climbed from sixth place to set an Asian Para Games record of 250.0 points, edging compatriot Avani Lekhara by just 0.4 points.Avani, the defending champion and a two-time Paralympic gold medallist, settled for silver with 249.6 points, giving India its first 1-2 finish of the day.Mona topped qualification with 629.1 points, setting an Asian Para Games qualification record, while Avani was second with 626.4.The victory also secured India a second quota place for the 2028 Los Angeles Paralympics. Mona had already earned one quota at the World Shooting Para Sport World Championships in Changwon, South Korea, last month, where she won silver.Nishad, Soumya and Rinku power athletics gold rushThe athletics arena delivered three gold medals and a series of podium finishes as India continued its strong start.Nishad, a two-time Paralympic silver medallist, produced a memorable performance to win the men’s T47 long jump with an effort of 7.11m. It was the Indian’s first international competition in the long jump, making his gold medal all the more special.Nishad lost his right arm in an accident involving a grass-cutting machine when he was six years old. He nevertheless dominated the competition, recording 7.11m twice to finish ahead of Uzbekistan’s Omadbek Khasanov, who won silver with a season-best 6.99m.Soumya added another gold in the women’s 1500m T12/T13 event, clocking a personal-best 5:12.39. Running alongside guide Bharath Kumar, she finished ahead of compatriot Venkatesh Radha, who took silver in 5:30.90. The result gave India its second 1-2 finish of the day.Japan’s Mana Sasaki recorded a faster time of 5:12.15 in the T13 category but finished behind the Indian athletes in the combined event after the results were determined by classification-based points.India completed its third 1-2 finish in the men’s F46 javelin throw, where Rinku clinched gold with a season-best effort of 65.11m. Ajeet Singh followed closely with 65.02m, also a season best, to take silver. Indonesia’s Rizal Bagus Saktyono won bronze with a personal-best throw of 55.30m.India also won a bronze in the women’s 1500m T11 event through Ravanni Valasanaini, who clocked a personal-best 5:41.85 to finish third. Her compatriot Rakshitha Raju, who recorded a faster time of 5:31.45, was disqualified.Judokas add silver and bronze; swimming chips inIndia’s visually impaired judokas contributed two more medals. Kokila won silver in the women’s J2 -52kg category after losing to Kyrgyzstan’s Aibike Ulanbek Kyzy in the final.Kapil Parmar claimed bronze in the men’s J1 -70kg division. After losing his semifinal 0-1 to Indonesia’s Junaedi, Kapil bounced back in the bronze-medal playoff to beat another Indonesian, Ahnaf Rafli Shidqi, 1-0.India’s medal count rose further when Ravi Karthik Budigina won silver in the men’s 100m freestyle S13 para swimming event. He clocked 56.68 seconds to finish behind Uzbekistan’s Egor Bolotov, who won gold in 52.90 seconds. Kazakhstan’s Viktor Volkov took bronze in 57.23 seconds.These results took India’s confirmed medal haul to four gold, five silver and two bronze by the end of the opening day.Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news, check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Sindhu, Mirabai in IOA electoral roll; Lovepreet’s doping past raises questions
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Olympic and world medallists PV Sindhu and Saikhom Mirabai Chanu headline a star-studded list of athletes cleared to contest the Indian Olympic
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Olympic and world medallists PV Sindhu and Saikhom Mirabai Chanu headline a star-studded list of athletes cleared to contest the Indian Olympic Association's (IOA) Athletes’ Commission elections on Nov 3, with weightlifter Lovepreet Singh’s doping past raising questions over his inclusion.The final electoral roll, approved by returning officer Sanjay K Srivastava, IAS (retd), also features Asian Games gold-winning hockey captains Harmanpreet Singh and Salima Tete, shooting sensation Neeru Dhanda, archery veterans Abhishek Verma and L Bombayla Devi, shot putter Tajinderpal Singh Toor, badminton's Kidambi Srikanth, fencer C A Bhavani Devi, rugby captain Nasser Aga Hussain and wrestler Aman Sehrawat.However, Lovepreet’s inclusion has drawn scrutiny. He tested positive for a prohibited substance at the senior Nationals meet in Visakhapatnam in Feb 2019 and was provisionally suspended by the National Anti-Doping Agency (NADA) in July that year. He later returned to competition, featuring at the 2022 CCWG in Birmingham.The Athletes' Commission eligibility declaration states: “I have never been sanctioned for a violation under the WADA Code or the NADA Act, 2022 or for a breach of any applicable integrity regulation”. His inclusion raises questions over the Indian Weightlifting Federation's (IWLF) nomination of his name and there's a high possibility that the electoral officer will cancel his eligibility and seek a fresh name.The draft roll, published on Oct 12, listed nominations from 19 NSFs. The final list has 17, with the Basketball Federation of India’s nominees Ram Kumar Gahlawat and Manisha Satyajit Dange, and the Kabaddi federation’s Balwan Singh and Mamatha, excluded.Of the 34 NSFs listed as IOA members, only 17 have nominees in the final roll. They are archery, athletics, badminton, bowling, cycling, fencing, handball, hockey, kayaking and canoeing, netball, rowing, rugby, shooting, squash, swimming, weightlifting and wrestling.The elections will determine athlete representation in the IOA’s Athletes’ Commission.Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news, check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: LA28 Olympics: Great Britain fourth in men's team final at Gymnastics World Championships
articles.summary: Great Britain just miss out on earning a spot at the 2028 Olympic Games at the first attempt, placing fourth in the men's team final at the Gymnastics World Championships.
articles.body:
Great Britain narrowly missed out on qualifying for the 2028 Olympic Games at the first attempt as they placed fourth in the men's team final at the Gymnastics World Championships.

Only the top three in Rotterdam were assured of early qualification for the Games in Los Angeles in two years' time, with defending champions Japan taking the gold medal ahead of Russia in second and China in third.

GB's next chance to qualify will be at the World Championships in Chengdu, China in 2027, where a top-nine finish will secure a place in LA.

Courtney Tulloch, Joe Fraser, Jake Jarman, Harry Hepworth and Reuben Ward qualified in second place for the final and finished with a total score of 247.395 on Tuesday.

The team were leading the standings after four of the six rotations, but they just fell short of staying in the medal places as Japan, Russia and China all improved in the closing stages. Japan took the step on the podium with a score of 251.928.

Fraser told BBC Sport the team feel they are in a good position to challenge for titles in the future.

"I think collectively, as a team, we can look at the overall of the team final and know that we are definitely amongst the best in the world, and we can compete with the best in the world," Fraser said.

"We were taking Japan right the way to the end, and up until the parallel bars, we were with them.

"So we know as long as we can work on our routines from the parallel bars and the high bar, we can really contend to be world champions maybe next year."

You can watch coverage of the Gymnastics World Championships, which run until Sunday, 25 October, on BBC Two and BBC iPlayer.

articles.title: 86 kg Preview & Predictions - 2026 Senior World Wrestling Championships
articles.summary: A full preview with predictions for the 86 kg weight class at the 2026 Senior World Wrestling Championships.
articles.body:
The 2026 Senior World Championships will take place in Astana, Kazakhstan from October 24-November 1 and will be streamed live on FloWrestling. The 86 kg weight class in the men's freestyle division competes October 30-31, and will feature Team USA's Kyle Dake searching for his 3rd world title at his 3rd different weight. Dake will be challenged by Olympic champion Magomed Ramazanov, world champion Kamran Ghasempour, and several other world class wrestlers. Check out the article below for a full preview with predictions for what has the potential to be the best weight class at Worlds this year!

*Of note - the World Championship rankings are based on head-to-head match results. The seeds are based on points accumulated at UWW Ranking Series Tournaments, the 2025 World Championships, and the 2025 Continental Championships.

86 kg World Championship Projected Seeds

The above five wrestlers are all legitimate threats to win a title this year at 86 kg. Of these 5, 3 are world/Olympic champions (Magomed Ramazanov, Kamran Ghasempour, and Kyle Dake), and Arsenii Dzhioev is a world medalist. Ibragim Kadiev is the only non-senior world medalist but is only 22 years old, a two-time U20 World Champion, and one of Russia's brightest prospects. The level of high-level talent leading this weight is truly remarkable and will make 86 kg one of the best weights to watch at Worlds this year.

Magomed Ramazanov leads this group as the 2024 Olympic champion but missed almost all of last year due to injury. Back in action this year, Ramazanov has notable victories over Aeoden Sinclair (6-3), Bolat Sakayev (8-2), and Abdulmuslim Abdulmuslimov (5-0). Despite those victories, Ramazanov forfeited in the finals of the Stepan Sargsyan Cup (to Amanula Gadzhimagomedov) and in the finals of the Ulaanbaatar Open (to Mohammad Nokhodi). It's been a long time since Ramazanov's been tested against one of the best in the world. Ramazanov's lack of high-level competition makes me uncertain about what to expect from him at Worlds, but if he wrestles like he did 2 years ago, Ramazanov has the ability to stand atop the podium in Astana.

Magomed Ramazanov's win in the 2025 European Championships finals over Magomedkhabib Kadimagomedov:

Russia's Ibragim Kadiev has the potential to be Russia's next superstar. He's a two-time U20 world champion and has notable senior-level victories over Artur Naifonov (three times), Kyle Dake, Khidir Saipudinov, Arsenii Dzhioev (two times), Georgios Kougioumtsidis, and Vladimeri Gamkrelidze. In total, that's 4 different world medalists and 2 different world champs. Despite all of that success, Kadiev is 0-2 in his career against Kamran Ghasempour and recently lost to Zahid Valencia at RAF Moscow. Kadiev will be the #3 seed and will likely have to get by Ghasempour in the semis this year. Will Kadiev rise to the incredible expectations placed on him, or will he fold under the pressure again this year?

Kadiev's win over Kyle Dake at the 2026 Muhamet Malo:

Arsenii Dzhioev won world bronze last year but is still largely unknown by most casual freestyle fans. Dzhioev is 14-2 over the past year, with his only losses coming against Ibragim Kadiev (3-2 and 2-1), and he has notable victories over Kamran Ghasempour, Khidir Saipudinov, Akhmed Usmanov, Vladimeri Gamkrelidze, Kyle Dake, and Artur Naifonov. Dzhioev is also notably the last wrestler to defeat Trent Hidlay - a 5-0 decision that came back at the 2025 Zagreb Open. Those results have moved Dzhioev all the way up to #14 in our pound-for-pound rankings and make him a legitimate threat to win gold this year.

Arsenii Dzhioev's win over Kyle Dake at the 2026 Muhamet Malo:

Kamran Ghasempour is already a two-time world champion at 92 kg (2021 and 2022) but is still looking for his first title at 86 kg. Ghasempour finished with a bronze medal last year after losing to Zahid Valencia in the World semis (7-0), while recording victories over Mukul Dahiya, Ibragim Kadiev, Bambilguun Naadambat, and Mukhammad Abdullaev. It's been more than 4 years since Ghasempour won Worlds, and this year will tell us if Ghasempour can get back on top or if his best days are behind him.

Ghasempour's win over Ibragim Kadiev at the 2025 World Championships:

Kyle Dake is 35 years old and is remarkably looking to win a world title at his third different weight class. Dake, a two-time world champion at both 74 kg and 79 kg, made the world team this year by defeating defending world champion Zahid Valencia in an outstanding best-of-three series at this year's Final X. Beyond those wins, this year Dake also has significant victories over Khidir Saipudinov, Aeoden Sinclair, Parker Keckeisen (twice), Magomedkhabib Kadimagomedov (twice), and Vladimeri Gamkrelidze. Though Dake dropped matches to Ibragim Kadiev and Arsenii Dzhioev in February, I wouldn't be surprised to see Dake avenge those losses in Astana. Those matches were highly competitive, and Dake is known for his ability to make adjustments and avenge losses the second time he wrestles an opponent. Considering the past results and accolades of the wrestlers, if Dake wins this bracket, it will be the greatest performance of his senior-level career.

Kyle Dake's three-match series against Zahid Valencia at Final X:

2023 world silver medalist Vladimeri Gamkrelidze leads this group of medal contenders based on his results over the past year. Gamkrelidze placed 2nd at the Zagreb Open, 3rd at the European Championships, and 1st at the Budapest Ranking Series Tournament. Along with those tournament placements, Gamkrelidze recorded notable victories over Zahid Valencia, Rakhim Magamadov (twice), Eugeniu Mihalcean, Abolfazl Shamsipour, and Osman Gocen. As important as those wins are, it's important to note Gamkrelidze's only losses this year are to Parker Keckeisen (4-3), Arsenii Dzhioev (6-4), Ibragim Kadiev (9-4), and Kyle Dake (2-0). Gamkrelidze is just a slight step behind the title contenders at 86 kg, and if there's going to be an upset in this bracket, Gamkrelidze is the one that could pull it off.

Malik Shavaev, a Russian now representing Kyrgyzstan, has never competed at a World Championships but notably won Russian Nationals back in 2021. In that tournament, Shavaev defeated world bronze medalist Radik Valiev and world champion Akhmed Usmanov. That was the best performance of Shavaev's career, but it wasn't a one-off performance. Shavaev has been active this year, competing in 6 different international tournaments and placing in 5 of those 6 tournaments. That level of consistency at a weight this deep is noteworthy and makes Shavaev a real threat to make a deep run in this bracket.

Georgios Kougioumtsidis is the final wrestler in this field that should be considered a legitimate medal threat. Kougioumtsidis won the 79 kg world title last year but has struggled slightly moving up in weight this year. Kougioumtsidis is only 6-5 since the 2025 World Championships and has yet to record a win over a world medalist at 86 kg. World-class wrestlers struggling slightly while moving up in weight isn't uncommon, and I wouldn't be surprised to see Kougioumtsidis right the ship at Worlds.

Kougioumtsidis' win in the 2025 World finals over Levi Haines:

There are some really strong wrestlers in this field, including Khidir Saipudinov, Bolat Sakayev, Rakhim Magamadov, and Boris Makoev. All of these wrestlers have been in the game for a while and have some legitimate accomplishments. However, in a field this deep, I don't consider those four wrestlers to be medal contenders, and they're certainly not "sleepers." The above two wrestlers fit this final category much better.

Natsura Okazawa finished third at the 2026 U20 World Championships this year with victories over Askhab Khajiyev (who just beat Zahid Valencia), Diachi Papinashvili (13-2), Tejvir Dhinsa (10-0), and Arun Arun (10-0), while only losing a close 7-6 match to Aeoden Sinclair. Okazawa has potent leg attacks highlighted by his strength and speed. Even in his loss to Sinclair, Okazawa got out to a quick 6-0 lead off three takedowns, and Sinclair looked like he had no answers for Okazawa's offense. Okazawa's one weakness is his poor cardio, but if he can shore up that weakness, Okazawa has the skills to defeat one of the contenders in this field.

Ismail Kucuksolak is another wrestler that fits the "Sleepers & Landmines" category. Kucuksolak is coming off a silver medal at the 2026 Mediterranean Games, where he lost to Georgios Kougioumtsidis in the finals but defeated Gabriel Iglesias and Rakhim Magamadov. On top of that performance, Kucuksolak placed third at the Budapest Ranking Series Tournament in July, losing only to Malik Shavaev but defeating Krisztian Biro and Eugeniu Mihalcean. I wouldn't pick Kucuksolak to medal in this bracket, but I think he can defeat some of the more experienced and credentialed wrestlers at 86 kg.

86 kg might be the most challenging weight for me to predict of the entire World Championships this year. I could make a legitimate case for each of the five title contenders to win gold this year. I've gone back and forth, but I'm picking Ibragim Kadiev to win gold in Astana. I think Kadiev has the best offense of anyone in the bracket, and since he's so young, I think he's only getting better. Is Kyle Dake good enough to win? Absolutely. However, I'm leaning toward youth over experience to win this bracket in Kazakhstan.

articles.title: From husband and wife to business partners: How Neeraj Chopra and Himani Mor are building a sports business to create a lasting legacy
articles.summary: Neeraj Chopra has spent years perfecting the art of throwing a javelin beyond 90 metres.
articles.body: Neeraj Chopra has spent years perfecting the art of throwing a javelin beyond 90 metres. Now, India's golden boy is pursuing a different kind of ambition — building a sports business that can outlast his competitive career. And he is doing it alongside his wife, Himani Mor, who is not merely his life partner but the managing director of his new venture, Vel Sports.Launched in January 2026, Vel Sports marked a significant turning point for the Olympic and world champion, who ended his decade-long association with JSW Sports to establish his own athlete management firm. For Chopra, the move was about creating a trusted team that would allow him to concentrate on competition while laying the foundations for his legacy.For Mor, a former international-level tennis player with an academic background in sports management, the appointment was an opportunity to turn her own experiences as an athlete into a business philosophy: one that puts athletes' needs before commercial demands.Together, they want Vel Sports and the Neeraj Chopra Foundation to contribute to a stronger sporting ecosystem in India, helping athletes succeed both on and off the field. Their partnership is built around a shared understanding of elite sport, but also on a clear distinction between their professional responsibilities and personal relationship.From a sporting connection to marriage and businessThe story of Chopra and Mor began well before they became one of Indian sport's most recognisable couples.Both hail from Haryana — Chopra from Panipat and Mor from Sonipat — and their families had known each other for years. Their connection dates back to 2016, before Chopra became an Olympic champion.“We have known each other since 2016, before he won the junior World Championship,” Mor told The Indian Express, recalling their early association through the Sports Authority of India's training centre in Sonipat.Sport was a natural meeting point. Mor came from a family with a strong sporting background. Her cousins competed in wrestling and boxing, while her parents played kabaddi. Her father captained the Indian team at the first circle kabaddi World Cup in Pakistan in 1983.“There was a common interest. You talk to each other, get to know each other, and that's how our relationship started. Our families were aware. That's how we got married,” she said.Mor describes their marriage as a fusion of an arranged and a love marriage. They tied the knot in a private ceremony in Solan in January 2025.Their relationship subsequently evolved into a professional partnership, with Chopra launching Vel Sports in January 2026 and appointing Mor as managing director. He brought the experience of competing at the highest level and navigating commercial partnerships, while she brought an athlete's perspective combined with formal training in sports management.Why Neeraj Chopra wanted his own sports businessChopra's decision to establish Vel Sports came after a decade with JSW Sports, which supported his rise from a promising javelin thrower to an Olympic gold medallist at Tokyo 2020, a world champion in 2023 and an Olympic silver medallist at Paris 2024.His departure from JSW Sports was described by both sides as a respectful conclusion to a successful association. Chopra acknowledged the role the organisation had played in his career, while the company expressed pride in their shared achievements.But the next phase of his journey demanded a different approach.“Another reason for starting Vel Sports is because Neeraj wanted his own trusted team to take care of everything. He wants to focus on the sport,” Mor explained.Chopra remains an active athlete, but his ambitions extend beyond medals and records. He wants to create an organisation that can continue contributing to Indian sport after his competitive career ends.“He might have another six years as an athlete. At this stage, throwing ninety metres is just a number. But he wants to create a legacy,” Mor said, while speaking to The Indian Express.“He is now looking at breaking records and not just about winning a gold. He wants the next generation to have the mindset that they can win at the highest levels of sport and stay at the top.”That vision is central to Vel Sports. Rather than treating athlete management simply as a business of securing sponsorships and endorsements, the company intends to build a system in which commercial opportunities complement sporting ambitions.The athlete-first philosophy behind Vel SportsFor elite athletes, commercial commitments can be both an opportunity and a challenge. Brand campaigns, appearances and promotional obligations can generate income and build a public profile, but they must be balanced against training, recovery and competition schedules.Mor believes the people managing those commitments need to understand what an athlete's daily life involves.“We want to keep athletes and their priorities at the forefront,” she said.“We want to create an ecosystem that works around athletes' schedules, allows them to balance their training while also maintaining their professional commitments. Being athletes ourselves, we understand what it takes to perform at the highest levels and what approach is best for an athlete. Because one missed session can cost them a lot.”The objective is to ensure that athletes and brands benefit without compromising sporting performance.Chopra has expressed a similar view, drawing on the lessons of his own career. At the beginning, he said, he did not have enough knowledge about competition planning or working with brands. Vel Sports is intended to help athletes navigate those areas with greater support.The model is not entirely new internationally. Athletes such as LeBron James, Lewis Hamilton and Coco Gauff have pursued business ventures while continuing their sporting careers. In India, Sunil Gavaskar co-founded Professional Management Group during his playing days in the 1980s.Chopra's move places him within that tradition, with the added ambition of building an athlete-focused business in a country where sporting careers can be shaped as much by access to resources and professional guidance as by talent.Beyond Vel Sports: Building a legacy for Indian sportThe couple's ambitions extend beyond athlete representation. The Neeraj Chopra Foundation aims to support emerging athletes and contribute to India's wider sporting ecosystem.One initiative is the Indian School of Coaching Excellence, launched in collaboration with badminton coach Pullela Gopichand's Badminton Gurukul and AISTS INDIA in August 2026. It aims to improve coach education through multidisciplinary programmes covering sports science, physical literacy, technology and athlete development.The underlying belief is that India's future sporting success depends not only on identifying talented athletes but also on giving them access to knowledgeable coaches and effective support systems.The foundation has also joined the Indian Olympic Association in a Clean Sport anti-doping awareness initiative. Chopra's experience as an athlete who has competed at the highest level gives him a platform to promote clean sport.For the couple, these projects represent different parts of the same vision: better management for established athletes, more support for emerging talent and stronger systems around the people responsible for developing champions.Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news, check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Japón, nueva prueba para las 'Guerreras' antes del Europeo
articles.standfirst: La selección española femenina disputará este jueves y el próximo sábado dos amistosos ante el combinado nipón en el Bolaños de Calatrava
articles.summary: La selección española femenina disputará este jueves y el próximo sábado dos amistosos ante el combinado nipón en el Bolaños de Calatrava
articles.body: Las Guerreras se preparan para afrontar una nueva prueba en su camino hacia el Campeonato de Europa. La selección española femenina, dirigida por Joaquín Rocamora, se medirá a Japón en un doble compromiso amistoso que tendrá lugar este jueves y el próximo sábado, a partir de las 18:00 horas, en el Pabellón Municipal Macarena Aguilar de Bolaños de Calatrava (Ciudad Real). El horizonte de las Guerreras está fijado en el Europeo de 2026, donde España competirá en el Grupo C de la fase preliminar frente a Dinamarca, Turquía y Grecia. El campeonato, que se disputará del 3 al 20 de diciembre en cinco países, será además una cita clave en el camino hacia Los Ángeles 2028, ya que la selección campeona obtendrá la clasificación directa para los Juegos Olímpicos. Las Guerreras llegan a esta cita después de medirse a Alemania, vigente subcampeona del mundo, en un doble enfrentamiento disputado en el Palau d’Esports de Granollers. España cayó por poco en el primer duelo (29-31), pero reaccionó en el segundo para firmar una importante victoria por 35-30. Un resultado que permitió al equipo cerrar la concentración con buenas sensaciones y dar continuidad al trabajo desarrollado por el cuerpo técnico. Japón será ahora el siguiente desafío para las internacionales españolas, que buscarán trasladar a la pista los avances de las últimas semanas y continuar ajustando su juego ante un rival de características diferentes. El historial de enfrentamientos entre España y Japón refleja un balance favorable a las Guerreras. Desde 2007, ambas selecciones se han enfrentado en ocho ocasiones, con siete victorias para el combinado español y una única derrota, registrada en el Torneo Internacional de España de 2023, celebrado en Santander. Más allá de los precedentes, el doble amistoso ofrecerá una nueva oportunidad para poner a prueba los recursos del equipo y continuar acumulando experiencia internacional antes de afrontar el reto europeo. Los dos partidos permitirán, además, seguir evaluando la evolución de las jugadoras y reforzar los automatismos colectivos de cara a la cita continental. articles.title: German triathlon boss to run for DOSB presidency
articles.summary: German Triathlon Union (DTU) chief Martin Engelhardt will run again for the presidency of the German Olympic Sports Confederation (DOSB), it was announced on...
articles.body:
German Triathlon Union (DTU) chief Martin Engelhardt will run again for the presidency of the German Olympic Sports Confederation (DOSB), it was announced on Wednesday.

The DTU has submitted the election proposal together with other DOSB member federations for Engelhardt to run against Michael Mronz, a member of the International Committee (IOC) who was proposed by a selection committee of German sport.

Mronz has good Olympic connections through his IOC role which could help Munich's bid for the 2036, 2040 or 2044 Games.

The DOSB president is elected on December 5 at its assembly and will succeed Thomas Weikert, who is not seeking another term.

Engelhardt is making a second attempt for the DOSB presidency. He lost in 2018 against Alfons Hörmann.

Engelhardt said he would be fully available from April 2027 after ending his profession as head physician at an Osnabrück hospital. He was DTU president 1987-2001 and again since 2011, is a DOSB vice president and was a doctor on the 2004 and 2008 German Olympic teams.

"I know the sport inside out, from club level right up to the world governing body, through research into high-performance sport and from having been at two Olympic Games alongside our athletes," Engelhardt said.

"I would like to put forward a proposal to the German sporting community that reflects its diversity: a sports strategy for Germany, which we will implement in collaboration with politicians, with the aim of tackling major national and international challenges in a united and successful manner."

articles.title: Anna Morris: World champion's medical career still 'on pause' for Olympics
articles.summary: Dr Anna Morris’ Instagram bio still says "career as a doctor on pause" as she targets the 2028 Olympic Games.
articles.body:
Dr Anna Morris' Instagram bio ends with "career as a doctor on pause".

It was only meant to be for a year. But five years on and it's still on hold.

Having watched the Tokyo Olympics as a junior doctor in hospital, Morris decided to take a break from her medical career and, after enjoying cycling as a student, go all in on the sport. She dreamed of competing for Wales and Great Britain.

She has just won three world titles to cement her status as one of the very best in the world.

Morris' golds in the team pursuit, omnium and madison meant she became the first woman to win all three events in a single championships since the introduction of women's madison in 2017.

"It's pretty high up there with one of the best years on my bike so far," Morris told BBC Sport Wales, after she also won two golds and a bronze at the Commonwealth Games in the summer.

"There's such strong depth in the women's field at the moment. There's some really good names in the field.

"You never know how you're going to fare up against them, so to come away with three golds, I'm still struggling to find the words."

Morris had not even been in a velodrome before she was 20.

Now 31, her rise to the top of the world has been remarkable. She won the world individual pursuit title in 2024 before she had even won the British national championship.

At each competition, and as each year passes, she seems to get better.

Now the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics are in her sights.

"It's down to hard work and consistency over time," she continued.

"Being part of British Cycling, you're among the best in the world and you can really learn off that.

"And I think that, when you enjoy what you do, when you're passionate about what you do and you put the hard work in, one thing's just led to the next.

"I think there's still more to come, hopefully."

After years of dominance, it has felt like the rest of the world has caught up with Great Britain over the last few campaigns.

But the team returned to the top of the medal table at the World Championships, despite their top male sprinter Matt Richardson having to withdraw amid an alleged misconduct investigation.

Morris won her golds in the women's team pursuit, omnium and madison (alongside teenage debutant Erin Boothman).

She did not ride one of her strongest events - the individual pursuit - only to see her team-mates Millie Couzens and Josie Knight take gold and silver.

"It is hard," Morris admitted. "You could probably field a few different teams that could all get the same result.

"So it is difficult when it comes down to selection, but as a team it's such a good place to be in.

"You're trying to be the best in the world at something so to have that depth and strength in your squad is just amazing, getting to train with each other, and it definitely contributes to their overall team performance."

The World Championships represented the first step on the qualification process for the 2028 Olympics.

And so, for at least another two years, Dr Morris' medical career remains on hold.

articles.title: Beth Dobbin writes to Andy Burnham calling for increased funding into ME research
articles.summary: Former British sprinter Beth Dobbin calls on Prime Minister Andy Burnham to fund more research into "life-decimating" ME.
articles.body:
Former British sprinter Beth Dobbin has called on Prime Minister Andy Burnham to fund more research into the "life-decimating" condition that has resulted in her spending 22 hours a day in bed.

On Friday, 32-year-old Dobbin - who raced at the Tokyo Olympics five years ago - revealed in an interview with BBC Sport she had been diagnosed with ME (myalgic encephalomyelitis).

ME is a chronic, fluctuating disease, causing symptoms such as sleep problems, problems with thinking and memory, pain and severe, persistent fatigue that does not improve with rest, and more.

It has no known cure or specific treatment. More than 400,000 people in the UK are thought to have ME, although the true figure could exceed one million, with severity ranging from people able to work or study to those requiring round-the-clock care and tube feeding.

In a letter to Burnham , external , Dobbin said: "ME has been neglected and psychologicalised for years.

"It has received so little government funding for research over the years compared to other illnesses. As a consequence, there are no approved treatments.

"There are also currently no provisions within the NHS for severe ME patients (25% of those with ME). What other illness this prevalent would leave patients with nowhere to go within the NHS, or no specialists other than to seek private care?"

The Olympic sprinter now bedbound for 22 hours a day

ME patients often rely on off-label medication to manage a condition that can cause more than 200 symptoms, including nausea, headaches, poor cognitive function and brain fog.

A conversation, or even something so simple as a light too bright or a sound too loud, can cause a "crash" that lasts 24, 48 hours, or in the worst cases, months on end.

Dobbin, who has left the house on just five occasions this year, decided to do the interview with BBC Sport in a bid to raise awareness of the condition, despite knowing it could trigger a brutal deterioration in her health.

"Your government has said it wants to bring down the welfare bill," Dobbin continued in her letter to Burnham.

She added: "ME is so debilitating, severe patients are violently unwell, bedbound and can't even look after themselves, let alone work.

"To get the welfare bill down, I believe you need to fund research into this spiralling illness and help us all get our lives back."

Since becoming prime minister in July, Burnham has vowed to reduce the UK's welfare bill.

Spending on benefits has ballooned in recent years and is forecast to rise to £408.6bn in 2030-31, according to figures from the Department for Work and Pensions.

Between April 2019 and March 2024 the UK government invested around £6.5 million in research into ME.

Earlier this year, when Sir Keir Starmer was prime minister, it announced an investment of £4.75 million towards a world-first genomics study into the condition.

BBC Sport has contacted No 10 for comment.

articles.title: WNBA anthem controversy sparks calls to bar players who don't stand from Team USA's Olympic roster
articles.summary: Riley Gaines says Atlanta Dream and Golden State Valkyries players who skip the WNBA Finals anthem should lose Olympic eligibility for Team USA.
articles.body: The Atlanta Dream and Golden State Valkyries left the court for the national anthem before the first two games of the WNBA Finals. Now Riley Gaines is arguing that those decisions should carry consequences when athletes seek to represent the United States internationally. Gaines initially weighed in while sharing OutKick’s video of the Game 2 anthem absence. "It’s my personal opinion that if you kneel for the flag and what it represents, you shouldn’t be able to represent the USA at the Olympics," Gaines wrote on X. DREAM, VALKYRIES SKIP NATIONAL ANTHEM IN WNBA FINALS GAME 2 DESPITE RULEBOOK REQUIREMENT In a statement to OutKick, Gaines expanded her argument to players who leave the court to avoid the anthem. "The American flag and our national anthem do not represent whichever political party or administration happens to be in power. They represent the American people, our shared identity, the freedoms we enjoy, and the generations of men and women who fought, sacrificed and died to preserve those freedoms," Gaines said. "Players who leave the court specifically to avoid the national anthem are making a deliberate statement. They are free to do so, of course. Free speech includes the freedom to withhold respect." "But I’m of the mind that choice has consequences when the same athletes later seek the honor of representing the United States on the international stage." Neither Finals team nor the WNBA has answered OutKick’s questions about the anthem absences. Nor has the NBA, whose commissioner, Adam Silver, is helping lead the search for the WNBA’s next commissioner. NBA STAYS SILENT ON WNBA FINALS TEAMS SKIPPING NATIONAL ANTHEM IN GAMES 1 AND 2 Gaines said patriotism does not require blind allegiance to a political party or pretending America is without flaws. But she argued that athletes seeking to represent the country should be judged on how they treat its anthem. "If an athlete treats standing for the anthem as optional or objectionable during the WNBA season, it is reasonable to question whether they are prepared to accept the full weight of representing the country when the spotlight is global," she said. Former Georgia state Rep. Vernon Jones called Tuesday for players from both teams to lose their eligibility to represent the United States in Olympic basketball. Jones wrote that those players "should be ineligible to play on the U.S. Women’s Olympic Basketball Team." Atlanta’s Team USA connection includes Angel Reese and Rhyne Howard Reese and Howard were both named to Team USA’s 2026 Women’s World Cup roster. The Dream announced their selections in August, noting that they became the first two players in franchise history selected together for the United States at a five-on-five Women’s World Cup or Olympics. Golden State had no players on that U.S. World Cup roster, but Valkyries head coach Natalie Nakase served as a U.S. assistant coach. Golden State star Gabby Williams represents France. Both Reese and Howard stood for the national anthem while representing the United States at September’s FIBA Women’s World Cup. AMERICA'S WOMEN'S BASKETBALL EPIC REACHES CLIMAX WITH NATIONAL UNITY ON THE LINE IN FIBA WORLD CUP FINAL But representing the United States internationally comes with an extra responsibility to show respect for the country at home. And that responsibility doesn't disappear when the USA jersey comes off and the WNBA jersey goes on. Staying off the court while the anthem plays during the WNBA Finals falls short of the standard we should expect from athletes entrusted with representing this country. Sage Steele warns anthem absences could drive fans away Former ESPN anchor Sage Steele also criticized the league in a social media video. Steele accused the WNBA’s players, coaches and leadership of disrespecting the country by leaving the court for the anthem. "So are they free to express themselves the way they want? Absolutely. But there’s a cost to it," Steele said. "And I just hope they realize that this constant lack of respect is going to turn fans away forever. They’re not going to come back, and it’s going to be their own fault," Steele added. Players are free to express themselves, but as Steele noted, that freedom can come with a price. We're not calling for the players to be jailed. The First Amendment limits the government’s power to restrict speech, but it doesn’t require fans to support those choices or critics to stay quiet. We have the right to express our disapproval, too. WNBA rulebook calls for an anthem lineup Both Finals teams were off the floor during the anthem before Saturday’s opener and Monday’s Game 2 at Chase Center. In both games, the players returned within seconds of the performance ending. The WNBA’s 2026 official rulebook includes a provision calling for players, coaches and trainers to stand and line up in a dignified posture along the sidelines or foul line during the national anthem. OUTKICK IS NOW AVAILABLE ON THE FOX NEWS APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD OutKick contacted the WNBA and both teams after Game 1, followed up Sunday and again Tuesday. The inquiries sought explanations for the absences, clarification of the league’s anthem requirements and the teams’ plans for Game 3 on Wednesday night in Atlanta. Those questions remain unanswered. For Gaines, the responsibility goes beyond a WNBA pregame routine. "Wearing the USA jersey is not a private entitlement that comes with athletic success. It is a public responsibility," she said.

articles.title: Aichi-Nagoya: Japan is known for world-class events - but the Asian Games were chaotic
articles.summary: Hotel chaos, transport mishaps and diplomatic blunders cast a spotlight on organisers and the firm hired to deliver the games.
articles.body:
From the Olympics to Tokyo's annual video game convention, Japan has a strong track record of hosting major international events. But this year's Asian Games in Nagoya and the wider Aichi Prefecture were marred by problems.

There were diplomatic blunders, transport errors and accommodation chaos. In comment fields online, some branded it the "worst Games in history" and urged a "full investigation".

Prof Kozo Tomiyama, who studies major sporting events at Osaka University, believes organisers were unable to handle the unexpected.

"If these problems damage international confidence in Japan's ability to operate sporting events, they could also affect Japan's ability to attract international competitions in the future," he warned.

The deputy director general of the Games, Takaaki Omi, admitted organisers had faced a range of unforeseen issues, but insisted they took on feedback and made improvements.

Before the tournament had even begun, participants were complaining about too few rooms and poor-quality accommodation.

Organisers had decided to forgo building a traditional athletes' village to cut costs, and were instead housing participants in hotels and container-style units across Nagoya. A top Korean basketball official said tall athletes housed in the containers were struggling to "stretch their legs out on the beds" .

Last-minute additions to the total number of participants strained the city's capacity so much that an Italian cruise ship with 1,500 cabins was used to fill the gap.

The organising committee had initially arranged accommodation for up to 15,000 delegation members "in accordance with the host city contract", Omi told the BBC. But as other sports were added, the number grew by 2,000 to a total of 17,000 .

Organisers initially claimed there was "simply nowhere" to put up the late influx and told them to make their own arrangements - before backpedalling and releasing a joint statement with the Olympic Council of Asia promising that all "17,000-plus" guests would get "Games-appropriate accommodation".

This was just the start of the problems.

Over the course of the Games, athletes were bussed to the wrong venues and the North Korean anthem was played for the South Korean men's hockey team . During the men's football gold medal ceremony, the South Korean flag was not raised properly. Taiwan's sports minister found himself temporarily barred from a flag-raising event.

In the last days of the Games, volunteers received an email inviting them to the closing ceremony free of charge. But later an organiser said the decision to distribute free tickets was still under review and had not been approved.

Omi admitted the string of incidents at the event - which was bigger than the Paris Olympics by number of participants - had caused significant inconvenience for some delegations.

"Hosting and managing an event of this scale was a major challenge for us, and each day involved addressing a range of unexpected issues and challenges," he said.

"During the Games, we also listened carefully to feedback from the athletes who were actually using the facilities and responded promptly with necessary improvements and measures."

As soon as these issues began to surface, local media pointed fingers at the company managing venue operations: the Japanese subsidiary of France's GL Events.

GL Events had won the 63bn yen (£306m; $405m) contract over Dentsu Group, an advertising giant with a long history of successfully running sporting events in Japan that had been sidelined after a criminal bid-rigging conviction.

A source told Kyodo news agency that GL Events was "overwhelmingly cheaper" than alternative providers.

Last week the Tokyo Shimbun newspaper accused the firm of aggressively cutting corners on hiring, resulting in a shortage of experienced staff capable of managing the issues which arose. The personnel that were recruited were not properly trained, the newspaper alleged.

But organiser Takaaki Omi stressed that GL Events "has experience in international sporting events, including the Paris Olympic Games".

"We believe the necessary competition environment was in place by the start of competition, including thorough discussions and co-ordination with GL Events," he told the BBC.

Prof Tomiyama said he didn't think it was right to "simply conclude that GL events did not have sufficient experience with international competitions". He believes the issue stemmed from the "extremely broad" scope of responsibility they were given.

"Also, because this was a negotiated contract rather than a competitive tender, it's important to examine the criteria organisers used to assess the contractor's capabilities, as well as how they supervised the contractor after the contract was awarded," Tomiyama added.

GL Events did not respond to repeated BBC requests for comment.

Watching organisers play whack-a-mole as they rushed to address each new concern which popped up throughout the Games felt deeply out of line with what the world has come to expect from a major Japanese event.

It's far from the "omotenashi" spirit - Japan's whole-hearted hospitality that is almost an art form - they might have wanted to showcase.

Officials ended up having to send a formal apology to South Korea for the series of mishaps affecting that particular delegation.

But Olympic Council of Asia director general Husain al-Musallam was keen to highlight the 54 new world records achieved at the Games - in swimming, weightlifting, and shooting - as proof they were a hit.

"This achievement does not come without the best environment that the organising committee created for the athletes," he said. "The athletes cannot perform if they don't sleep good, the athletes cannot perform if they don't have good transportation."

While the Games may be over, the problems aren't.

Glitches have continued at the ongoing Para Games, where the wrong national anthems were played at three events. Nagoya Mayor Ichiro Hirosawa, who is also deputy head of the Games organising committee, called it "unacceptable" and offered his apologies.

Prof Tomiyama hopes organisers will take lessons from the past few weeks to deliver higher-quality sporting events in the future.

articles.title: Helsinki le gana el pulso a Bruselas y será la sede del Europeo de 2030
articles.standfirst: Será la cuarta vez que la capital finlandesa, sede también del primer Mundial en 1983 y los Juegos Olímpicos de 1952, acoja este campeonato
articles.summary: Será la cuarta vez que la capital finlandesa, sede también del primer Mundial en 1983 y los Juegos Olímpicos de 1952, acoja este campeonato
articles.body: Helsinki (Finlandia) acogerá una cuarta vez el Europeo de atletismo al aire libre. Será en 2030, a dos años vista de los Juegos Olímpicos de Brisbane (Australia). Así lo ha decidido el Consejo de European Athletics en Lausana (Suiza), en una votación en la que superó a Bruselas, la otra ciudad que había presentado una candidatura para este campeonato. Esta será la cuarta vez que los Campeonatos de Europa de Atletismo se celebren en la capital finlandesa —tras las ediciones de 1971, 1994 y 2012—, lo que convierte a Helsinki en la ciudad que más veces ha acogido este evento, cuya historia se remonta a 1934. Los Campeonatos de Europa de Atletismo de 2030 tendrán lugar en el histórico Estadio Olímpico de la ciudad, que reabrió sus puertas en 2020 tras una profunda renovación. En este mismo reciento se celebraron los Juegos Olímpicos de 1952, marcados por los tres oros del checoslovaco Emil Zatopek en 5.000, 10.000 y maratón. Además fue la sede del primer Mundial de la historia en 1983 y repitió fortuna en 2005, demostrando su estrecha vinculación con este deporte. Finlandia además fue la primera gran potencia del fondo mundial liderados por el mítico Paavo Nurmi, ganador de nuevo oros olímpicos en los años 20 del siglo pasado. Cabe recordar que antes se disputará el Campeonato de Europa de Atletismo de 2028 en Silesia (Polonia), del 3 al 8 de junio, cinco semanas antes de la inauguración de los Juegos Olímpicos de Los Ángeles. El Consejo de European Athletics también acordó que el Campeonato Europeo de Atletismo en Pista Cubierta de 2029 se dispute en Torun (Polonia), sede este mismo año del Mundial. La ciudad de Copérnico ya fue sede del Europeo indoor en 2021, en una campeonato marcado aún por las restricciones del COVID. Torun tomará así el relevo de Valencia, sede de este campeonato en 2027. En el Kujawsko-Pomorska Arena de Torun se han establecido tres récords mundiales, incluido el primero de los 15 récords mundiales de Armand Duplantis en salto con pértiga, cuando superó los 6,17 metros en febrero de 2020.

articles.title: Ruti Aga, ganadora del maratón de Tokio, sancionada seis años por dopaje
articles.standfirst: La etíope ha sido castigada por su positivo por metilprednisolona y la posterior manipulación de ciertas pruebas
articles.summary: La etíope ha sido castigada por su positivo por metilprednisolona y la posterior manipulación de ciertas pruebas
articles.body: La atleta etíope Ruti Aga, que había sido suspendida de forma provisional el pasado septiembre, ha sido sancionada seis años por la Unidad de Integridad del Atletismo (AIU, por sus siglas en inglés) debido a su positivo y a la posterior manipulación de pruebas. Así, la atleta, ganadora del maratón de Tokio en 2019, tiene una mejor marca personal en la distancia de 2.18:09 y ha subido en seis ocasiones al podio de los 'majors' durante su carrera deportiva. Aga dio positivo por este corticoides tras competir en el medio maratón de Xiamen (China) el pasado 15 de marzo, por lo que recibe una sanción de dos años. Los otros cuatro años de castigo impuestos por la AIU se deben a la manipulación de pruebas, ya que la maratoniana aportó una receta falsa de una clínica que no existía en su proceso de defensa, en el que alegó que su positivo se debía a un tratamiento para una lesión en la rodilla. "Hemos logrado avances significativos en la lucha contra el dopaje en el maratón durante los últimos seis o siete años, pero aún queda mucho por hacer", explicó Brett Clothier, director ejecutivo de la AIU. "Las investigaciones son fundamentales para descubrir el dopaje y desenmascarar explicaciones falsas. Proteger una competición limpia requiere recursos, pero este caso envía un mensaje claro: los intentos de hacer trampas quedarán al descubierto".

articles.title: Republican lawmaker believes the WNBA should adopt the Olympic standard for women’s sports
articles.summary: WNBA commissioner Cathy Engelbert told a congressman that Enes Kanter Freedom and Royce White aren't women but still won't define the term for the league.
articles.body: The WNBA is still having a heck of a time definitively saying what a woman is, but according to a letter from league commissioner Cathy Engelbert to Rep. Marlin Stutzman, R-Ind., former NBA players Enes Kanter Freedom and Royce White are not it â women, that is. Stutzman joined OutKick's Dan Dakich on the Wednesday edition of "Don't @ Me with Dan Dakich" to discuss it. Dakich asked the representative point-blank what the league needed to put in writing so that this discussion â which Dakich called "dumbest conversation ever" â could be put to rest. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE Stutzman had a pretty straightforward solution and one that would even allow the league to wipe its hands of criticism from the lefties by passing the buck. "Well, I think they could just follow another organization's definitions," Stutzman suggested. "Say they're going to follow the Olympics organization's definition. They don't even have to define it themselves â there are already other organizations that define what a biological woman is." That's about as easy as it gets. The International Olympic Committee took one on the chin from the pro-men in women's sports crowd, and, would you believe, the IOC is still, at last check, alive and kicking.
